newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesian economic policy on track after election.
newsitem.headline: Indonesian economic policy on track after election.

text.p: The Indonesian government is unlikely to make any major economic policy changes following general elections last week, but economic analysts said it should take note of some of the signals from the violence in the run-up to the polls.
The ruling Golkar, assured of victory before a vote was cast in Thursday's elections, swept just over 74 percent of the vote, up from 68 percent in the last poll in 1992.

"I don't see any real policy implication, because if anything the government can argue the increased share of votes justify the continuation of existing policy," Desmond Supple, Asia currency economist at BZW Barclays in Singapore, told Reuters.
Supple said policy changes would be on the margin rather than any alteration in the broad sweep of policy.

"Economic policy is still going to be a movement toward the continued liberalisation, continued effort at fiscal and monetary policy prudence. The economic backdrop for Indonesia is going to remain extremely favourable," Supple said.
But some analysts said the government should take account of the worst political violence of President Suharto's 30-year rule in the 27-day election campaign.

There was the fear of further violence if Golkar's runner-up and main contender during the campaign, the Moslem-oriented United Development Party (PPP), refused to accept its 23 percent share of the vote.
The only other party legally permitted to contests the poll, the badly-split Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), trailed far behind with three percent.
Mari Pangestu, acting head of the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said the government should have received signals from the violence of the campaign.
"I don't know whether the government would return to business as usual after the poll. But we have seen enough signals prior to the poll," Pangestu said.
She said the government should tackle the source of violence quickly, adding that the short-term worry was whether the PPP would accept the election outcome.
PPP campaign manager Jusuf Sjakir said the party will decide next Thursday on whether to accept the result following what he said were widespread irregularities during the election.

Analysts have blamed a series of riots over the past year -- mainly on Java island, home to 60 percent of the country's 200 million people -- on socio-economic tensions and urban poverty, frustration with an autocratic system and pervasive corruption.
The financial community was still nervous over the potential for further violence, watching the PPP reaction closely.
The rupiah in fact strengthened against the dollar following the poll, while the Jakarta stock market also rose. Some analysts expected a mixed week ahead before the market steadied again.
However, the macroeconomic picture appeared to be attracting investors.
Peregrine Securities said in a report there were not enough negatives in politics to justify staying out of a market backed by robust growth and sound economic management.
Indonesia's foreign exchange reserve rose steadily to $20.382 billion in April from $15.961 billion in April 1996.
Its current account deficit was forecast to stay at about four percent of GDP for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting April.
